#1002. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

What is the aim for Kompany, Kane and Bayern?

#1001. Brighton and Liverpool made unfashionable tactical pivots at the weekend that could be the start of a new trend

If these two clubs are doing it, it's worth investigating...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Crossing isn’t exactly a dying art, but it has certainly become rarer to see the more ambitious, attack-minded teams swing crosses into the box from open play.

It just isn’t de rigueur to try something so low-percentage, something so unfashionably anti-aesthetic.

But two of the most attacking clubs (with two of the most modern, zeitgeisty tacticians) pivoted to crossing at the weekend, so it is worth considering whether this is the beginning of a new trend that will catch on.

Fashion, after all, plays an outsized role in tactical theory in the Premier League, and if Brighton and Liverpool are doing it, then it must be Smart and Good.

Liverpool’s 12 open-play crosses in the first half on Sunday were the most any team have managed against Arsenal since November 2020. By the 42nd minute, when Alex Mac Allister should have scored with a header from what was their 19th cross (open or set-piece) of the match, Liverpool had almost quadrupled the five crosses they made in the whole game against Brighton the weekend before.

Brighton weren’t as consistent in their 2-0 victory over Manchester City, but there was a clear tactical plan to switch the play with long diagonals into the (very wide) wingers as often as possible. Fabian Hurzeler appeared to see City’s not-actually-full-backs as the weak spot, and it worked, leading directly to the winning goal.

Liverpool and Brighton had different reasons for their strategies, although the end result was the same: both knew that by getting balls into the box they could sew chaos. Brighton’s winner came via a deflected half-clearance, while Arsenal’s defence regularly made first contact but, now on the back foot, were penned in by the loose second ball (at their most dishevelled, Jurrien Timber pulled on Alexander Isak’s shirt).

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

As Iraola put it: “We’ve put them under pressure, we’ve put them inside the box, we’ve put them there.”

Arsenal, uncomfortable, were pushed back into the box; were 'put there'. It is a simple, albeit unfashionable, idea that others may choose to follow.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#1000. Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League

Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

"We are absolutely in love with him. He's been an incredible manager. The results are extraordinary and we're flying."

Those words from Ben Parker will be familiar to fans of any club who have been on the kind of winning run Brighton and Hove Albion are currently on.

But all the signs on and off the pitch suggest that the man in question — Brighton's German coach Fabian Hürzeler — is more than just a flash in the Premier League pan.

Hürzeler has never coached in Germany's Bundesliga. After winning promotion to Germany's top flight with St. Pauli in 2024, he left to become the youngest man ever to take charge in England's Premier League at 31. His team currently sit third, having won six games in a row including a 5-0 thrashing of bitter rivals Crystal Palace last weekend.

It was the repeat of a fixture last season that marked Hürzeler's lowest Brighton ebb, with a 1-0 home loss making it one win in 12. "There are only two options," the German coach said at the time. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Parker, the co-editor of Brighton and Hove Albion fanzine, Dogma, admitted to DW that there were plenty who weren't sure if persisting was the answer. "There was some disquiet at the end of that game, there were people shouting: 'You're getting sacked in the morning.'"

While such sentiment may be difficult to swallow for many coaches, Parker said that Hürzeler told him in an interview soon after joining the club that he welcomed it when needed.

"He talked about wanting a fan relationship that had a two-way aspect. The club and him are really ambitious, so if the performances aren't up to scratch, we should be telling him that. And that's what happened on that day. I see the whole thing as being quite healthy."

Hürzeler never played at the top level. He represented Germany's youth teams and turned out for Bayern Munich's reserves but soon grew frustrated with second-team football. He then accepted a player-coach role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23. From 2018, he was also an assistant coach for Germany's U20s.

He performed this alongside a job at an art dealership in the German state of Bavaria, where he moved with his family at the age of two having been born in the United States. After starting as an assistant coach at St. Pauli in 2020, he took over after head coach Timo Schultz was fired in late 2022. Since then, he hasn't looked back.

That unusual path to top-flight management and some innovative tactics at St. Pauli led to a perception in Germany that Hürzeler was a little aloof and something of a 'laptop manager' in the vein of former Bayern Munich and Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann who had a similarly nondescript playing career. This, so the charge goes, meant Hürzeler wasn't able to forge the relationships and togetherness needed to make a team more than the sum of its parts.

That was rarely what was reported by his players and staff at St. Pauli, nor is it Hürzeler's belief. "I want to be myself, I don't want to play a role, and my age definitely helps regarding understanding the players," he said.

"I always say I speak their language and I understand their thoughts, because it wasn't that long ago when I played."

His antics on the sideline also earned him a reputation as a bit of a hothead. Hürzeler was booked seven times during St. Pauli's promotion push and since joining Brighton, the German has been booked nine times and been sent off once. When asked about this, he said: "Emotions are part of the game."

Parker said this authenticity has also been reflected in his relationship with Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of England.

"For most Brighton fans he comes across as quite a quirky, interesting, left-field figure. The mantra he set out when he first arrived was quite counter-culturalist, to challenge the establishment, and that fits well here," Parker said.

"You will see him walking along on the seafront, going up for coffees around town, and he travels back and forth on an ebike, not in a chauffer-driven car as a lot of managers might. He's also hosted fan events in pubs, which I believe he paid for. So I'd say he's very approachable."

But Hürzeler isn't the only 30-something German beloved in Brighton.

Pascal Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, is also a firm favorite. The midfielder, who retired from Germany duty after the World Cup earlier this year, has scored three and made four in the club's opening seven league games. The 35-year-old's connection with Hürzeler is also key, with Groß admitting he stayed in touch with Hürzeler even before he resigned. The return is proving to look a great decision for both sides.

"I was here for seven years, got married here and both my kids were born in England. The most important milestones in my life happened here. I missed my friends and the feeling of being deeply connected to the club."

The feeling is mutual, said Parker. "Pascal Gross is everybody's favorite player. He's Brighton's first best signing, from Ingolstadt, and second-best signing, from Dortmund. He's a sensational player, and it's probably true to say there is a lot of warmth towards German football and Germany because of these hugely important characters at the football club."

The Premier League club's success has been built on a smart coach and player recruitment strategy guided by local owner, Tony Bloom. Part of the model is that those who shine brightest will often be snatched by the bigger fish.

"I think he's said he's a supporter of Bayern Munich, and he uses them as an example of the standards he wants," said Parker of Hürzeler. "I can see that he could be a good fit in a couple of years time. He won't go to a Liverpool or a Chelsea, I think there's a strong pull to Bayern in particular."

Bayern's current boss, Vincent Kompany, is in little danger at the moment, though Bayern coaches are only ever a few losses from crisis. For the meantime, Hürzeler is also happy where he is, having extended his contract to 2029. Again, the feeling is mutual.

Next up in the Premier League is a trip to Liverpool, where Jürgen Klopp became the first German coach to make a real mark on the Premier League. But before that, Hürzeler's team have an assignment in the Europa Conference League, a competition Brighton are among the favorites to win. Parker hopes a first major trophy is in sight.

"If he can be the person that wins us that first trophy, then he will go down as the greatest."

The Reds lost their way after the teenager’s withdrawal in Sunday’s defeat to Arsenal as the midfielder shone on his first ever Premier League start

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola grabbed Trey Nyoni and threw him in at the deep end. Sink or swim was the aim of the game. And the teenager kept his head above water, and then some.

The teenager made his first ever Premier League start on Sunday afternoon. The call was well deserved following a fine showing against Chelsea in the EFL Cup.

That it came against defending champions Arsenal was a huge show of faith in the midfielder. The Reds may have fallen to a narrow 1-0 home defeat to the Gunners, but Nyoni’s 59-minute display proved he’s ready for regular minutes in this Liverpool side.

You’d be forgiven for overlooking Nyoni’s showing at Anfield. Declan Rice, after all, was the star performer on Merseyside. Mikel Arteta’s ‘Master-of-all-Trades’ midfield man put in a dominant display in the middle of the park.

The assist for Kai Havertz’s one and only goal was the cherry on the icing atop the Arsenal cake.

Yet despite coming up against, arguably, one of the best midfielders in world football, Nyoni wasn’t overawed. Rather, he rose to the occasion to deliver a performance that perhaps convinced Iraola he is worthy of a starting spot at the expense of either Alexis Mac Allister or Ryan Gravenberch.

“I just tried to go out there and do what I do, tried to get on the ball as much as possible and bring the team forwards,” Nyoni told the official Liverpool website about making his debut in such a blockbuster event. Many would have been overwhelmed by the spotlight that came from such a moment. Nyoni, though, was buoyed on by the welcome of Arsenal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 19-year-old ended the game with the best pass success rate (96.4%) of all starters in Sunday’s match. Only teammates Virgil van Dijk (67) and Mac Allister (61) made more passes than the academy product (56). The former pair played the full 90, whereas the latter was withdrawn on the hour mark.

Nyoni was dictating the tempo in the middle of the park, and driving Liverpool forward. Only Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya (46) made more forward passes than the youngster (24) at the weekend. Fourteen line-breaking passes was the most during his time on the pitch.

Iraola’s decision to withdraw Nyoni in place of the returning Dominik Szoboszlai meant that, for a 15-minute spell, Liverpool ceded momentum as they struggled to gain a foothold on the game.

From the 76th-minute onwards, they again dominated possession, even if it amounted to nothing, but Nyoni’s substitution saw the tie swing back in Arsenal’s favour at a crucial time in the clash. It’s within this 15-minute window where Arteta’s men begin to turn the screw in games. Only Manchester United (33) have had more shots than Arsenal (26) between minutes 60 and 75. Twenty-four chances created ranks top.

Liverpool needed a player who was comfortable in possession to ensure Arsenal were unable to build upon Havertz’s early strike. Of course, the momentum swing didn’t amount to another Gunners goal. Conversely, Liverpool would have enjoyed a more comfortable period of play had Nyoni remained on the pitch.

He brings some much-needed composure in a key area, a quality that had been found wanting following the departure of Curtis Jones. The sidelined Ryan Gravenberch brings the drive from deep, while Mac Allister offers the nitty-gritty, off the ball work to help protect the defence. Nyoni, meanwhile, delivers the forward thrust with his vision and distribution, qualities that far exceed both Gravenberch and Mac Allister, particularly in a 4-2-3-1 setup.

And having been dispossessed just four times in all competitions this season, Nyoni’s press resistance is another important trait. He’s comfortable receiving the ball from the centre-backs, before turning and setting his side on the frontfoot. Even under pressure, you’d back the up-and-coming Reds star to wriggle his way out of danger.

At his age, Nyoni, physically, still has some growing to do. Iraola can be expected to manage his minutes accordingly in order to avoid injury stunting his growth. Regardless, it’s clear that Nyoni is ready for a more prominent role in this Liverpool side.

Former boss Arne Slot used Nyoni sparingly, despite speaking highly of the player. In a difficult second, and final, season in the Anfield dugout, the Dutchman opted for experience. Injuries have perhaps forced Iraola’s hand this time around, but Nyoni has grabbed the opportunity to consolidate a starting spot with both hands.

Ben is a freelance football expert with over 15 years of experience in the field, ranging from stats, to betting, to transfer analysis, to news, and everything in between. Having departed esteemed football stats website WhoScored.com in 2025, he has been touring the freelance circuit, and has been featured on The Guardian, The Independent, Sky Sports, The Premier League, TNT Sports, ESPN, Squawka and talkSPORT, among others.

#997. When is FA Cup second round draw? Ball numbers, time and how to watch

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The draw for the second round of the FA Cup will take place on Monday 9 November after this weekend’s fixtures

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The FA Cup is in full swing for the 2026-27 season with 40 first round fixtures to be played over the weekend before the draw for the second round takes place on Monday 9 November.

32 non-league sides remain in the competition and will be seeking to stake a claim for a spot in the next round as they come up against the teams from League’s One and Two.

Friday night’s matches see 2021 champions, and former Premier League winners, Leicester City take on the National League’s Oxford City while Bristol Rovers do battle with Cambridge United.

Over the weekend, there are exciting and intriguing fixtures across the board with the potential for the magic of the FA Cup to provide some upsets. League One’s promotion-chasers Bradford City host Marine FC while, AFC Rushden & Diamonds - one of four teams to reach this stage of the competition for the very first time - travel to Burton Albion.

Another of those first-time clubs is Sholing who face fellow non-league side Salisbury in a winnable fixture while the two remaining teams, Plymouth Parkway and Berkhamsted, conclude the first round fixtures on Monday evening and will contest a spot in the next round following the second round draw on TNT Sports.

Other teams of note are former FA Cup winners Sheffield Wednesday (1896, 1907 and 1935) who take on Oldham Athletic, Huddersfield Town (1922) who face Exeter City and Wigan Athletic (2013) who will travel to Boreham Wood.

Here’s everything you need to know about the second-round draw.

The draw for the second round of the 2026-27 FA Cup takes place on Monday 9 November, before the clash between non-league clubs Plymouth Parkway and Berkhamsted.

The television coverage of the game starts at 6:30pm BST, with the draw itself expected to begin shortly afterwards.

The draw will be available to watch live in the UK on TNT Sports 1, HBO Max, and on the TNT Sports YouTube channel. Coverage begins at 6.30pm, with the draw itself expected to start before kick off at 7.30pm.

There will be 40 teams in the draw for the second round with 20 fixtures to be made ahead of the entry of the Premier League and Championship clubs from the third round onwards.

The ball numbers for the draw will be revealed over the weekend closer to the time of the draw itself.

The 20 FA Cup second-round matches will be held across the weekend of 5-6 of December, with the third-round draw presumed to take place on the evening of Monday 7 December.

#996. Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year deal at Real Madrid in August

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?

#994. US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

#993. Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Bianca Nogrady is a freelance science journalist based in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, Australia.

Scientists say it is important to foster digital literacy and healthy online habits in those growing up using social media.Credit: StockPlanets/E+/Getty

In 1972, sociologist and criminologist Stanley Cohen published a book called Folk Devils and Moral Panics, which explored the concept of moral panic: the idea that societies periodically fixate on a newly emerged condition, behaviour, identity or community as being a threat to the public. The fixation is characterized by ‘handwringing’ and calls to action among societal leaders; a particular pattern of media coverage; and experts breaking down the problem and offering diagnoses and solutions.

Today, concerns about the impact of digital and social media on children and adolescents are never far from the headlines, but there is growing evidence that this isn’t simply another case of moral panic. Politicians, religious leaders and others have been speaking out with increasing intensity about how social media harms young people. And a growing volume of scientific literature is exploring the nature and prevalence of those harms, and what might be done about them1,2.

One thing that differentiates this case from moral panic is that young people themselves are worried, too. “It is not just older generations saying, ‘Kids, get off your screens’,” says Georgia Turner, a neuroscience researcher at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit at the University of Cambridge, UK. Work by Turner and her colleagues suggests that nearly half of adolescents think that they are addicted to social media.

“Whether or not they are correct about the use of the clinical terms, they are clearly unhappy with their screen use,” Turner says. “I would say that we should treat people believing that they have a problem as itself a problem or a concern that we need to try and understand.”

Scientists have directed considerable effort into understanding the nature of screen addiction. “We know that the adolescent period is a time of profound changes in how the brain is developing and responding to its social environment, to peers, to family context,” says psychologist and neuroscientist Eva Telzer, co-director of the Winston National Center on Technology Use, Brain, and Psychological Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. And now, during that important developmental stage, adolescents are spending more time on digital technology, and in particular on social media.

Concerned about how social media might be affecting children and adolescents, governments around the world are attempting to regulate or curtail its use. Last December, the Australian government implemented a social-media ban for those aged under 16, intended to prevent them from accessing or having accounts on social-media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X. Numerous European countries, including the United Kingdom, France and Italy, are attempting to follow suit.

The situation raises a fundamental question, Telzer says: “How can this social environment potentially be rewiring the developing brain during this really important period when the brain is so sensitive?”

From birth, the brain grows rapidly in size and connectivity as children learn and develop and neurons proliferate and form connections called synapses. But in early childhood, that growth is accompanied by what’s called synaptic pruning, during which neuronal synapses disconnect and are cleared away. At the end of this process, there are around 40% fewer synapses than at the beginning. Neurons also die in a process called apoptosis. At the same time, the remaining neurons in the brain build up their coat of insulating white matter, or myelin, which is crucial for efficient transmission of electrical impulses.

While synaptic pruning is happening, the adolescent brain is maturing one region at a time, and the order of that maturation doesn’t lend itself to calm and rational thought and behaviour.

The first region to mature is rich in receptors for the hormone oxytocin — which is important in social bonding — and dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with reward and pleasure. “It’s why every middle-school student wants to talk about who sits where in the cafeteria and who’s more popular than whom,” says Mitch Prinstein, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

The last brain region to develop is the prefrontal cortex, which is essential for decision-making, exercising judgement and processing emotions such as fear and happiness.

Unfortunately, that makes the adolescent brain vulnerable to some design elements of social media: comparison features such as likes, and addictive elements such as push notifications and endless scrolling. “Imagine in the 80s, there was skywriting across your neighbourhood that said the most popular kid in school is talking about you right now with most of the rest of the grade in your school,” Prinstein says. “You would run down the street looking for them in your neighbourhood — it would be impossible to resist that.”

Neuroscience researcher Georgia Turner says that adolescents can be sensitive to the dopamine-driven rewards offered by social media.

And that is exactly what social media does for adolescents, he says, describing it as a perfect, tragic storm. “This is what the brain is hypersensitive towards, while not able to stop itself because the prefrontal cortex — the brain’s brakes — are not fully developed until the mid-20s,” Prinstein says.

A big part of the problem is dopamine, a neurotransmitter implicated in a range of addiction disorders. Because of the order in which brain regions mature, adolescents are extremely sensitive and responsive to reward, and social media delivers that in abundance; every like, new follower, positive comment or interesting thing delivers a kick of dopamine, says Turner. We experience those rewards in real life, but at a much lower frequency than on social media.

And that poses a risk to the developing brain. “We do know that if you, for example, do really increase dopamine transmission, that can have massive effects — particularly at young ages – on the way that your brain matures, and then your cognitive control in adulthood, your inhibition, your sensitivity to rewards,” Turner says.

Telzer and a colleague carried out a study involving 79 children and adolescents and found that those who spent more time on their smartphones during school hours — most of it on social media — performed worse on a test that assessed how well they could control their focus and attention. The researchers suggested that the immediate rewards offered by social media could be conditioning adolescents to need constant stimulation, and as a result they find it harder to maintain focus3.

Another study, co-authored by Samson Nivins, a developmental neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, which followed more than 8,300 children for four years, found a linear relationship between social-media use and inattention symptoms4.

Researchers have also used imaging to look for brain changes associated with social-media use. Nivins and his colleagues used magnetic resonance imaging to look for brain changes linked to using social media, playing video games or watching television over four years in 1,462 participants in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study5. They found that children with higher social-media use showed a small but significant decrease in the volume of the cerebellum, a brain region that is known for coordinating movement and balance and that has a key role in cognition, memory and communication. “Why we are concerned is … the cerebellum is involved in all psychiatric disorders,” Nivins says, suggesting that this could be one mechanism underpinning the association between high social-media use and anxiety and depression.

Developmental neuroscientist Samson Nivins has used imaging techniques to explore how different types of screen use affect the developing brain.Credit: Senthil Kumar/Aswath Photo Studio

Social-media-linked disruptions to sleep in adolescents could also affect the formation of insulating myelin, a component of the brain’s white matter, which is crucial for efficient nerve conduction and healthy brain function. Poor sleep is associated with negative effects on the formation and maintenance of myelin. Research involving 976 children in the Adolescent Behavior Cognitive Development Study found an association between shorter sleep, worse white-matter organization, screen time and depressive symptoms in early adolescents. The paper also suggested that sleep duration and its effects on white matter mediated the association between increased social-media use and greater depression-related symptoms6. “Social media is the number-one reason why kids are not getting recommended sleep,” Prinstein says.

A Leicester City supporters’ group has urged fans to boycott the club’s home shirt after their sponsor, BC Game, announced a partnership with an “international porn star”.

BC Game, an online casino company who have been Leicester’s front-of-shirt sponsor for the past two years, unveiled Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie as an “ambassador” this week.

A suggestive video featuring Eva Elfie and a man arriving at her door delivering pizza accompanied BC Game’s announcement with the content creator, who also does live streams of video games. “Let the fun begin,” the announcement added.

The Foxes Trust said there has been “dismay and discontent” with BC Game since their sponsorship began and questioned why the club continues to be partners with a company that lost its UK operating licence almost two years ago .

The group said: “Most Leicester City supporters will know by now the Trust’s dismay and discontent with BC Game being our front-of-shirt sponsor. BC Game have now announced a new partnership with ‘international content creator and Esports personality’ Eva Elfie… who just happens to be an international porn star.

“From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values. Our first article in July 2024 said that ‘It doesn’t feel like who LCFC are to have a gambling website on our shirts and seems to be another step away from our ‘well-run family club’ reputation’.

“The club has not only partnered with a gambling company, but chosen one that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, has unanswered questions about the legitimacy of its funding and its origins, and allows clients to ‘game’ using cryptocurrencies.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Both gambling and pornography can have devastating impacts on people's lives, in particular young people.

“Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now? As always our message is, if you’re purchasing an LCFC replica shirt, opt for one that doesn’t have the BC Game logo on it.”

The former Premier League champions, who now play in League One after consecutive relegations, said they were aware of the BC’s partnership with Eva Elfie and had “raised concerns” with the sponsor.

A club statement said: “Leicester City Football Club recognises the concerns raised about recent developments involving our Principal Partner, BC Game. We have raised these concerns directly with BC Game and are continuing discussions with the company to explore a mutually acceptable resolution.”

The Foxes Trust said an end-of-season survey held in May showed 73 per cent of fans felt “negative” about Leicester’s association with BC Game, with just five per cent of feelings with “content”.

BC Game CEO Ali Muhanned said in a statement: “Eva has built an incredible relationship with the gaming and esports community through genuine passion and consistent content creation. We can’t wait to see what Eva brings to the BC Game community.”

Middlesbrough's star-studded side of the 1990s was not without its issues

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You have to keep in mind just how exotic foreign players were in the Premier League in 1996, when most sides were made up of British and Irish players, maybe with the odd Scandinavian here or there.

So it's not hard to see why Middlesbrough captured the imagination not just of their own fans, but neutrals too thanks to the signings of Italian superstar Fabrizio Ravanelli and Brazilians Juninho, Emerson and Branco.

And Boro's Australian goalkeeper at the time, Mark Schwarzer, admits that created a bit of a culture shock for all concerned.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: "I only played with Fabrizio Ravanelli for my first season there, but I never had any issues with him.

"He just had a level of demand and expectation of players, a level of professionalism that exceeded the norm in England at that time.

"That caused problems with some of the squad. There was also a communication issue with language.

"But it was two different footballing worlds and British players were still adapting.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"You look at what Arsene Wenger brought into Arsenal around diet, well-being and professionalism – that was still in its beginnings in England."

Unfortunately, 'professionalism' was not particularly a watchword for Emerson, who went missing from the squad on multiple occasions as the club increasingly struggled against the threat of relegation.

In Emerson's defence, his wife was reportedly to be desperately unhappy on Teesside - but after finally being sold to Atletico Madrid after another disappearing act following the club's relegation, the midfielder admitted the error of his ways.

Schwarzer said: "I don’t think anybody was surprised. Emo was a phenomenal player, but mad. You just couldn’t control him.

"Even though he went AWOL, everyone still loved him. It was one of those where you should be irate, but you couldn’t because he was such a good guy.

"You just wished that he’d been there for the team more often."

Arsenal star Mikel Merino has been linked with a return to his homeland

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The father of Arsenal star Mikel Merino has explained the conditions in which his son will depart the club.

Merino has established himself as a cult hero at Arsenal, playing as a makeshift centre-forward during injury crises and chipping in with vital goals, but since moving to North London in the summer of 2024, he hasn't established himself as a first choice in manager Mikel Arteta's midfield.

This has led to talk that he could depart the Emirates Stadium for a return to Spain, as he looks to play more regularly for club and country.

As relayed by Sport Witness, Spain manager Luis de la Fuente has relegated Merino to a substitute role with the national team, while the midfielder played just 193 minutes at the World Cup.

Last month, Merino's father – Angel Miguel, a former professional footballer himself – laid out the conditions for his son moving back to La Liga, claiming, “he’ll want to continue in that rhythm of competing in the Champions League and keeping that motivation”.

Spanish outlet La Razon has since reported that Atletico Madrid want to sign the La Roja star on loan with a purchase option.

The 30-year-old has started just once in the Premier League this term but started three of Arsenal's four Champions League games, with Arteta using him as an alternative No.10 option to Martin Odegaard.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

With Arsenal boasting the likes of Declan Rice, Martin Zubimendi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes in midfield, Merino's chances of starting regularly are slim, but Arteta has leaned on his hold-up play and close control to help see out matches this season, with the star appearing in every single fixture so far.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal value Merino as a key member of the squad, however, despite the limited minutes.

The Spaniard is one of Arteta's leadership group, taking the captaincy from Odegaard on occasion in the Norwegian's absence this season, with many suggesting that Merino will take up coaching in the future.

Merino's contract runs until 2028, but with Arsenal in no desperate need to raise funds or sell a player in his prime, they could still choose to hold on to the midfielder until the end of his deal.

No discussions have taken place about an extension for the midfielder.

Merino is worth €25 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Hull City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#989. Thomas Tuchel explains Cole Palmer omission: ‘He misses too many opportunities’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The England manager has opted to ‘trust’ the players who impressed him in the last squad, while also offering first-time call-ups to Josh King and Jobe Bellingham

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Tuchel says he has “enough” No 10s in his England squad without selecting Cole Palmer, who has paid the price for pulling out of the September camp last time out and missing “too many opportunities to impress”.

The Chelsea star was a notable omission from Tuchel’s 25-man squad ahead of the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain and he was available for selection. Tuchel criticised Palmer for missing “too many camps with injuries” following his withdrawal from last month’s group and the manager has opted to stick with many of the same players who impressed him last time.

Tuchel has named several No 10s in his group, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White, Eberechi Eze, Jude Bellingham, as well as first-time call-ups Josh King and Jobe Bellingham, who both offer versatility in his midfield.

Palmer has not played for England since March and was missed the World Cup after struggling with injuries last season. He has played in all nine of Chelsea’s Premier League matches this season, but was also sent off in the defeat to Tottenham.

Speaking at a press conference at Wembley, Tuchel explained: “It counts when you are in camp and I just said it last time, he misses too many opportunities to impress. It was a long camp. It was two-and-a-half weeks and the players and the boys who were in camp built something extraordinary throughout these weeks.

“That's why the credit goes to them. The trust is for them. If you are in camp, this is your chance to impress. So it's not personal. We will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset to come and desperate to play for his country, but the competition is on and the players who were in camp did an amazing job and kept their place.”

Tuchel added: “There are enough of No 10s, and we stick to the guys who were in camp because camp was excellent and we were happy with the last two-and-half weeks that we had together.

”The impact of all the players was immense throughout the whole camp and that's why we stick mainly with the group. We stick with all the offensive players and we have Josh King as a new player in there, but he can play four positions.”

Palmer was among five players to withdraw from Tuchel’s first England squad since the World Cup, along with Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento. Only vice-captain Rice, who featured heavily at the World Cup, has since been recalled.

Tuchel is not expecting as many withdrawals this time and said he will continue to reward the players who turn up for England and take their opportunities to shine, while adding that he believes his message is getting through to his players.

“It's always about the ones who are in camp,” he said. “It's always the ones who don't withdraw and who walk the talk and come to camp and show that it matters and put the quality in. This is always what we will reward.

“That was always the message very, very early since we took charge, that it matters if you are in camp and it matters what you do in camp. And the last camp was an excellent one.”

FourFourTwo's dedicated FPL columnist, and one of the top players in the world, BigManBakar selects his best differentials for GW10

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nine gameweeks in, the managers climbing the ranks are rarely the ones sitting on the same 15 players as everyone else.

Rank gains tend to come from backing someone the crowd has overlooked at the right moment. For this piece, a differential is any player owned by 15% or fewer FPL managers, and there are some strong ones available right now.

These are the six I would be looking at for Gameweek 10.

Thierno Barry (£5.6m, 7.6% owned) vs Coventry (h)

At £5.6m, Barry is some of the best value in the game, and the price alone makes him easy to fit in as an attacker for the weeks ahead. Only Erling Haaland has a higher Expected Goal (xG) involvement this season. People like to say he can't finish, but he scored eight from roughly 8.5 xG last year, which is hardly poor. Penalties could come his way as well, and Coventry at home is about as friendly as fixtures get.

Jarrad Branthwaite (£5.5m, 2.2% owned) vs Coventry (h)

Branthwaite is fit again and anchors an Everton side that has already kept four clean sheets. Coventry rank 20th for xG, and Everton carry some of the best clean sheet odds in the league. He also picks up defensive contributions, which gives him a solid points floor, and he is a differential route into the fixture that very few managers have noticed yet.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Luka Vuskovic (£5.2m, 7.4% owned) vs Brentford (h)

Expect Vuskovic to become hugely popular, especially with managers hunting an Ezri Konsa replacement. He is nailed on to play, good for defensive contributions, carries a goal threat and affordable.

Brighton are joint-top for clean sheets, and their schedule is strong, starting with Brentford at home this week before Hull City and Newcastle United in the weeks to follow.

Dominik Szoboszlai (£6.7m, 13.4% owned) vs Crystal Palace (a)

Szoboszlai is back and fit, which makes him a big differential again. He takes set pieces, might be on penalties and has bonus potential, so he has several ways to score points.

Palace have conceded more goals than any other side this season, and that gives his upside a nice boost for this one.

Matheus Cunha (£7.8m, 5.5% owned) vs Aston Villa (h)

Cunha scored twice in the Champions League against Roma and should be well placed for plenty of minutes against Villa. Man United have struggled in recent weeks, but a comeback like that against Roma could be just what they need to get going again. He is a fresh, lower owned way into a Man United attack that has been out of form but is far from short of ability.

Antonio Silva (£5.1m, 2.6% owned) vs Ipswich (a)

Silva has a good fixture this week and a very strong run directly after it. Bournemouth are in the top three for xG Conceded (xGC), even after a tough opening run in the first eight gameweeks. He is a near-certainty to start, good for defensive contributions and has encouraging underlying numbers for attacking threat, so he has plenty of routes to points.

At 2.6% ownership, he is one of the cheapest ways to get ahead of the field at the back.

Cristiano Ronaldo international curtain call is a bitter affair and sorry stain on one of the greats' legacies

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To the very end, Cristiano Ronaldo wants ownership of the narrative.

Ahead of Jorge Jesus' Portugal squad announcement for the upcoming November international break, Ronaldo has officially retired from the international side of the game.

Ronaldo's retirement statement was polished and studio-produced, framing his departure from international football as a considered, dignified decision of a man bowing out on his own terms. But nobody in football should be fooled by the PR surrounding his Portugal farewell. Ronaldo is not walking away because of his obligation to 'hand back the No. 7 shirt'; he is jumping before he's pushed.

With Portugal’s squad announcement for the November international window imminent, whispers had grown impossible to ignore, especially after the histrionics which made headlines during the most recent international break.

For everything we know about Ronaldo and the opinion he holds of himself, the prospect of reading a squad list without his name on it would have been unbearable.

No matter how it's dressed up, his exit from the international scene is an undignified end for a footballer of his stature, burning the house down rather than accept that time had finally caught up with him.

The genesis of the split came during the conjoined September and October international camps, where Ronaldo's conduct reflected entitled petulance. He could have chosen to be an experienced mentor to one of Europe's most gifted squads, but instead behaved emotionally, putting self before side.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

When substituted early during Portugal's Nations League fixture against Wales, the 41-year-old trudged off, held his tongue but not for very long.

From the outset, Jesus had made it clear that Portugal’s tactical system would no longer be warped to accommodate Ronaldo. The new coach wants aggressive front-foot pressing, off-the-ball running, and quick transitions, which Ronaldo is simply incompatible with. Tensions reportedly grew in training over Ronaldo’s lack of engagement in defensive drills and his habit of dropping deep into midfield spaces, disrupting the collective shape to hunt for touches.

"After the National Team Coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I made the decision to leave the National Team camp," Ronaldo wrote in a statement after being left out entirely against Norway. "In due time, I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself. Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

The ensuing media storm hijacked Portugal’s camp leaving teammates fielding questions about their captain's bruised ego rather than their own football.

That the curtain falls in this manner is a tragedy for international football. His 146 goals, 234 appearances, alarming longevity and bordering-on-delusional drive made him more than a footballer. Even his detractors will concede, he's earned the right to a fairytale farewell, which no doubt would have been a tearful, adoring lap of honour in Lisbon, where his career began over 20 years ago.

Now, though, he slips out through the side exit, some might say motivated by spite and wanting to save face. There will be no emotional testimonial or triumphant send-off, at least not yet. Cristiano Ronaldo may have spared himself the humiliation of being dropped, but in doing so, has traded in his hero’s goodbye.
